full_judgment:
Md Mozammel Hoque J: These two First Appeals namely, First Appeal No. 85 of 1997 and First Appeal No. 158 of 1999 are directed against the judgment and decree passed on 24-3-1997 by the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 1 of 1996. Since these two appeals have arisen out of the same judgment of the trial Court they were heard together and disposed of by one judgment. Defendants are the appellants before this Court and the plaintiff is the respondent in these two appeals. 

 8. Considering the material evidence on record and hearing the parties the trial Court decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff and it was decreed to the effect that the defendants No. 1 and 2 are bound to sell the suit property to the plaintiff at a highest tender money as offered by the highest tenderer defendant No. 3. Being aggrieved by this Judgment and decree the defendant No. 3, the highest tenderer has preferred First Appeal No. 85 of 1997 and defendant Nos. 1 and 2 have preferred First Appeal No. 158 of 1999. Since both the appeals have arisen out of the same judgment and decree of the trial Court these two appeals were heard together and are being disposed of by one judgment. 

 10. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Attorney-General appearing for the appellants in First Appeal No. 158 of 1999, submits that the plaintiff had no existing legal right to sue against the defendants at the relevant time i.e. on 3-8-1986, in view of the fact that at that time the plaintiff had no locus standi to sue against the defendants. Mr Mahmudul Islam further submits that through tender the Government proposed to sell the suit property and the defendant No. 3 had given the highest offer to purchase the same and that was accepted by the defendant Nos. 1 & 2. As soon as the offer was given and it was accepted by the Government it became a concluded contract and, as such, the defendant No. 3 had got a legal right to sue against the defendants Nos. 1 and 2 by way of specific performance of contract. Since it is a concluded contract and since the Government had no objection to sell the suit property to the defendant No. 3 the plaintiff had no right to challenge such a sale through tender. He further submits that the Government sold the, suit property under Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Buildings in the Urban Areas) Rules, 1972. Since the provisions of these rules have been followed the plaintiff is not entitled to have a decree over such property. He further submits that rule 10 of Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Buildings in the Urban Areas) Rules, 1972 was amended vide Gazette Notification dated 1st November. 1987 and the amendment was numbered as rule 10(4A) 'which runs as follows: 

 20. We have gone through the judgment and decree of the trial Court. It appears to us that the trial Court has considered each and every aspect of the case. Further, if appears that on considering the material evidence on record, both oral and documentary, the trial Court passed a decree in favour of the plaintiff. Mr Mahmudul Islam fails to point out any legal infirmity in the judgment of the trial Court. Mr Mahmudul Islam lastly, has raised a technical objection that on the basis of prayer as made in the plaint, a decree in the present form cannot be given. We have gone through the plaint including the prayer portion of the plaint and it appears to us that this objection being highly technical has no substance at all. The trial Court, in our view, has not committed any error either on facts or on law and, as such, the decree passed by the trial Court does not call for any interference by this Court. 

 22. In the result, both the appeals namely, First Appeal No. 85 of 1997 and First Appeal No. 158 of 1999 are hereby dismissed without any order, as to costs and the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court are hereby maintained. 

 25. The trial Court decreed the suit declaring that the plaintiff is entitled to purchase the suit property at the highest price quoted by defendant No. 3 in the tender and that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are obliged to sell the said property to him according to the terms and conditions of the tender. 

 In view of above legal position, the learned Subordinate Judge in decreeing the suit on 24-3-97 did not commit any error of law calling for our interference in any way and, as such, both the appeals therefore must fail.
